$comment: Sales proposal. Not a signed contract — a pitch that becomes one if accepted, which is why it ends in an acceptance signature block rather than mutual covenants. Reuses the commercial package's existing questions (company, counterparty, role, dealSize, industry, serviceDesc) rather than asking new ones, so choosing 'the proposal' out of the commercial package costs the user nothing extra. Drafting only, jurisdiction-neutral; numbers that are business judgements (validity window, response date) are bracketed blanks.

clauses.title: Introduction
clauses.rationale: The provider-side variant: this is your proposal to the counterparty. A short, human opening — the rest of the document is where the substance lives.
clauses.body: {{company}} is pleased to submit this proposal to {{counterparty}} dated {{date}}. It describes the work we propose, what it costs, and how to move forward.

clauses.title: Introduction
clauses.rationale: The client-side variant: you are requesting or receiving the proposal from the counterparty, so the sentence names them as the one proposing.
clauses.body: This proposal is submitted by {{counterparty}} to {{company}}, dated {{date}}. It describes the work proposed, what it costs, and how to move forward.

clauses.title: Background
clauses.rationale: Offered, not automatic — some proposals need a paragraph of context, and some are better off going straight to scope.
clauses.body: [A short paragraph on the situation or need this proposal responds to — what prompted it, and why now.]

clauses.title: What Is Proposed
clauses.rationale: The core of the pitch, in the user’s own words from the wizard, so the proposal describes the actual offer rather than a generic placeholder. Included only when the wizard's optional offer description is filled in.
clauses.body: We propose the following: {{offerDesc}}. This proposal covers {{industryName}}; anything outside that scope would be a separate discussion.

clauses.title: What Is Proposed
clauses.rationale: The offer description is optional in the wizard, because forcing every commercial-package user to describe an offer just to generate an NDA makes no sense. When it is left blank, the proposal still has a labeled place to write the offer directly on the page.
clauses.body: We propose the following: [describe the work or offer]. This proposal covers {{industryName}}; anything outside that scope would be a separate discussion.

clauses.title: Deliverables
clauses.rationale: Offered as a structured list for proposals with concrete outputs; not every proposal is deliverable-shaped, so it is not forced in.
clauses.body: What is delivered: [list the concrete deliverables — e.g. a discovery report, a design system, a final build]. What is not included: [name anything a reader might otherwise assume is covered, and is not].

clauses.title: Approach
clauses.rationale: Offered for proposals that want to show methodology, not just output — often what actually differentiates one proposal from a competitor’s.
clauses.body: How we would approach this: [describe the phases, methodology, or process — this is where a proposal can show its work, not just its price].

clauses.title: Investment
clauses.rationale: Anchors the price to the deal-size range the wizard already asked, so a proposal is never generated with pricing left silently blank. The exact figure is still the user’s to fill in — the range only sets the neighborhood.
clauses.body: This proposal is offered in the {{dealSizeName}} range. The exact price: [amount], payable [schedule — e.g. 50% to begin, 50% on completion]. Prices exclude taxes unless stated otherwise.

clauses.title: What’s Included
clauses.rationale: Offered for proposals priced in tiers or packages — makes the comparison legible instead of burying it in prose.
clauses.body: What the price includes: [list]. Optional add-ons, priced separately: [list, or “none”].

clauses.title: Timeline
clauses.rationale: Dates in a proposal are estimates until both sides sign something — the clause says so rather than implying a commitment the proposal alone does not make.
clauses.body: Proposed timeline: [key milestones and target dates]. Dates are estimates until confirmed in a signed agreement, and depend on a timely start and timely feedback from {{counterparty}}.

clauses.title: How Long This Proposal Is Open
clauses.rationale: Prices and availability change — an expiry date protects the proposer from being held to old numbers indefinitely, and gives the reader a reason to decide.
clauses.body: This proposal is valid until [date], [30] days from the date above. After that date, we are happy to revisit it, but the terms may change.

clauses.title: Next Steps
clauses.rationale: Tells the reader exactly what happens after they say yes — the difference between a proposal that gets acted on and one that sits in an inbox.
clauses.body: To move forward: sign and return this proposal, or confirm in writing that you accept it. We will then send [a Statement of Work / a Service Agreement / an invoice for the deposit] to formalize the engagement. Accepting this proposal is not itself a binding contract for the work — that comes from the agreement it leads to — but the signature below confirms mutual intent to proceed on these terms.

clauses.title: Questions
clauses.rationale: Offered as a small closing courtesy — not every proposal needs it, and it is easy to add or drop.
clauses.body: Questions about this proposal can go to [name, email, or phone]. We are glad to walk through any part of it before you decide.
